strengths: Significant scale: 4M examples across 20 tasks (9.36× larger than MMTab) with 88% original visualizations, addressing a real gap in existing VTU datasets
Well-executed retrieval of original table visualizations from archived Wikipedia using sound methodology (Levenshtein similarity with 0.70 threshold and Wikipedia API versioning)
Strong extensibility design: each example linked to source datasets, HTML serializations enable task reformulation, unified format supports future research

Comprehensive experimental validation: improvements on both held-in and held-out benchmarks, with models trained on TABLET outperforming 0/1-shot on 12/14 tasks, including degradation analysis showing robustness (6.63pp vs 28.9pp baseline)
Thorough documentation and reproducibility: full hyperparameters, GPU accounting, dataset variants (S/M/L) for computational trade-offs, multiple ablations

Honest presentation: clear comparison with MMTab, acknowledgment of limitations (data contamination, incomplete ablations, single model focus), and practical trade-off analysis between dataset size and performance
weaknesses: Weak empirical support for core claim: Table 2 shows minimal benefits of original visualizations on held-in benchmarks (WikiBio +1.9pp, WikiTQ -2.3pp, TabFact +1.6pp), with paper acknowledging that existing benchmarks lack visual reasoning requirements, undermining the primary motivation

Unaddressed data contamination: 61.5% of tables from Wikipedia (ubiquitous in pretraining), yet no investigation of contamination effects on Wikipedia-sourced benchmarks (WikiTQ, WikiBio, ToTTo) that dominate results

Incomplete ablation studies: authors explicitly state computational constraints prevented full per-task ablation; only 3 dataset sizes and 1 task category ablation tested, limiting understanding of which components drive improvements

Limited methodological novelty: primarily dataset aggregation with rephrased existing instructions; only one model fine-tuned (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) with zero-shot evaluation on others insufficient to demonstrate value; no advanced SFT techniques explored

Missing mechanistic analysis: no investigation of which visual features are actually utilized by models, why synthetic sometimes outperforms original (Table 2), or error analysis comparing original vs. synthetic conditions

Insufficient evidence for visual reasoning claims: no creation of visual-reasoning-specific tasks or analysis demonstrating that models leverage original visualizations rather than solving tasks through instruction-tuning alone; acknowledged but unresolved

strengths: Substantial scale (4M examples, 2M tables) with meaningful technical effort to preserve 88% original visualizations from Wikipedia using archival APIs and edit-distance matching
Comprehensive dataset design with 20 diverse tasks across multiple categories, full traceability via source IDs/HTML, and extensible annotation format
Thorough experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions including original vs. synthetic visualizations, dataset sizes, task balancing, and held-in/held-out benchmarks
Well-executed engineering with careful handling of Wikipedia table retrieval timing and metadata preservation enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Core claims inadequately supported: Table 2 shows original visualizations outperform synthetic in only 2/8 tasks, match in 4/8, and underperform in 1/8—directly undermining the primary motivation

Severe data contamination risk: Qwen2.5-VL-7B almost certainly encountered Wikipedia during pretraining; authors acknowledge portions of held-out test sets may have been seen during pretraining, compromising validity of benchmark improvements

Marginal practical benefits relative to computational cost (4000 GPU hours for TABLET-L); improvements are modest and confounded by distribution matching rather than evidence of genuine visual understanding gains

Incomplete ablations: Authors explicitly state they did not conduct full task ablation due to computational constraints; missing error analysis, case studies, and mechanistic insights into when original visualizations help
Severe task imbalance unresolved: Entity Linking comprises 54.2% of training data; TABLET-M's capping is a band-aid rather than principled solution; impact on transfer learning unclear
Limited fine-tuning scope: Only Qwen2.5-VL-7B fine-tuned; zero-shot results on other architectures (Tables 11-12) show highly variable performance, limiting generalizability claims
Overstated SOTA claims: Abstract claims 'state-of-the-art on 10/14 benchmarks' but comparisons are only against zero-shot Qwen2.5-VL, not comprehensive evaluation against other published VTU methods

Concerning finding inadequately addressed: Section 3.4 notes models ignore tables when highlighted cell values are mentioned in prompts, indicating poor visual grounding, but this is not thoroughly investigated
No systematic evaluation of which visual features matter: The paper lacks case studies, error analysis, or ablations examining which aspects of original visualizations provide value

strengths: Addresses a real problem with careful execution: preserves original table visualizations from real-world sources (Wikipedia, PubTabNet, TabMWP) rather than synthetic renderings, with thoughtful curation using version history APIs and edit-distance matching
Impressive scale and scope: 4 million examples across 20 diverse tasks from 14 source datasets, representing substantial aggregation work

Thoughtful extensible dataset design: provides both HTML serializations and images, comprehensive metadata, traceable links to source examples, enabling future reformulation and reducing researcher lock-in

Comprehensive experimental validation: rigorous comparison of original vs. synthetic visualizations, held-in and held-out evaluation, dataset sizing ablations (TABLET-S/M/L), robustness analysis, and zero-shot evaluation on multiple open-weight models
Excellent documentation: detailed appendices with task definitions, collection timelines, examples, and statistics; companion figures effectively illustrate dataset construction
Strong empirical results: fine-tuned models achieve state-of-the-art on 10 out of 14 benchmarks with consistent improvements on held-out tasks, suggesting genuine generalization benefits
Demonstrated robustness improvements: Table 9 shows models trained on original visualizations degrade only 6.6-7.9 percentage points when switched to synthetic images, compared to 28.9 for baselines
weaknesses: Core claim lacks strong empirical support: Table 2 shows lossless models match or underperform synthetic models on 5 of 8 held-in tasks. Original visualizations provide clear benefits only for robustness, not downstream task performance, weakening the main motivation

Inadequately addressed data contamination: 61.5% of tables from Wikipedia (likely in pretraining corpora for VLMs). Strong zero-shot performance on held-out tasks (e.g., 64.5% InfoTabs) suggests possible data leakage, dismissed in Section 9 without rigorous analysis

Limited architectural diversity: fine-tuning only on Qwen2.5-VL-7B; other models evaluated zero-shot only. This undermines claims of general utility and raises questions about whether benefits transfer across VLM families

Imbalanced and questionable task distribution: 54.2% from three 'table interpretation' tasks (entity linking, column type, relation extraction) that authors acknowledge 'do not represent downstream applications'
Limited methodological novelty: primarily dataset aggregation and curation rather than methodological innovation. Levenshtein similarity matching for table retrieval is straightforward, not novel
Missing critical ablations: no individual task contribution analysis due to computational constraints. Without these, understanding which components drive improvements is limited

Insufficient visual understanding analysis: no investigation of which visual features (colors, merged cells, fonts) help; no failure mode comparison between original and synthetic; claim that highlighting causes task-solving without table understanding (Section 3.4) lacks validation

Experimental design issues: TABLET-Bmix outperformance could result from additional training data (747k examples) rather than the mixture itself; no quantity-controlled ablation. Mixed metrics across tasks make overall progress difficult to assess
Incomplete related work engagement: MMTBench mentioned but not directly compared; limited empirical comparison with MMTab beyond size metrics

Reproducibility barriers: 4000 GPU hours for full fine-tuning exceeds most researchers' budgets; dependency on proprietary Qwen implementation reduces transparency; unclear design choices (0.70 Levenshtein threshold) lack justification

strengths: Addresses critical gap in VTU datasets by preserving original table visualizations (88% of 4M examples) rather than relying on synthetic renderings, with clear empirical benefits
Impressive scale and comprehensiveness: 4M examples across 21 tasks from 14 datasets, covering diverse table understanding categories
Rigorous construction methodology with careful historical tracing of Wikipedia tables, extensible metadata, and full source traceability

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 15 benchmarks (8 held-in, 7 held-out) with SOTA on 11/15; demonstrates both robust improvements on real-world visualizations (6.63-point degradation vs. 28.9-point baseline) and strong transfer to unseen tasks
Well-designed ablations and analysis (original vs. synthetic, dataset size variants, task contribution analysis, visual complexity analysis)
Novel VisualTableQA benchmark with 306 carefully annotated examples requiring joint visual-structural reasoning; fine-grained categorization aids interpretability
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, comprehensive appendix with task definitions and visual complexity metric specifications, code availability promised
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily aggregates existing datasets and preserves visualizations—a straightforward engineering contribution rather than methodological advance; no new tasks, architectures, or model innovations
Data contamination concerns inadequately addressed: most seed datasets from Wikipedia likely in pretraining corpora; no systematic analysis of overlap; could have reported model pretraining dates

Incomplete analysis due to computational constraints: full task ablation not conducted; design choices (why these 14 datasets?) not fully justified; limited investigation of which visual features drive improvements
VisualTableQA benchmark limitations: only 306 examples (small for generalization claims); no inter-annotator agreement reported; limited comparison to related visual reasoning benchmarks
Generalization concerns: main fine-tuning on single architecture (Qwen2.5-VL-7B); other models evaluated only zero-shot; results may not extend to future VLM architectures
Visual complexity metric appears ad-hoc with manually chosen weights; no human validation that complexity scores correlate with task difficulty; missing user studies to establish meaningfulness
Comparison with MMTab conflates dataset size and visualization quality; controlled comparison using equal-sized subsets with original visualizations would better isolate benefits
Missing error analysis, feature importance investigation, and analysis of which visual elements (colors, images, formatting) are most important for different tasks
Synthetic table quality (12% of examples) not validated; limited discussion of whether synthetic renderings adequately preserve original layout

strengths: Addresses genuine gap in VTU datasets by preserving 88% original visualizations instead of synthetic renderings
Large-scale dataset with 4M examples across 21 tasks and 2M unique tables, representing substantial effort
Comprehensive evaluation across 8 held-in and 7 held-out benchmarks with multiple model architectures
SOTA results on 11/15 table understanding benchmarks demonstrate utility and effectiveness
Well-designed for extensibility with HTML serializations, metadata, source links, and unified task format
Thorough robustness analysis showing original visualizations reduce degradation (6.63 vs 28.9 points) compared to synthetic renderings
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution is dataset aggregation and visualization retrieval rather than new methodology, architecture, or algorithmic innovation
Central claim undermined by 12% synthetic tables (747k examples, 18.4% of total); no analysis of retrieval failures or their impact on results
Unfair comparison with MMTab: simultaneously changes visualization quality AND dataset size (9.38x larger), confounding factors; can't isolate visualization contribution
Data contamination concerns unaddressed: Wikipedia tables likely in pretraining corpora; held-out validity questionable, but no empirical mitigation provided
Weak understanding of why original visualizations help: claims about visual features (ruling lines, colors) are asserted but not empirically validated; visual complexity metric lacks human validation
Task distribution heavily skewed: Entity Linking 35.3% of training data, Table Interpretation 54.2% total—these don't represent downstream applications despite ablation showing utility
Experimental inconsistencies: Qwen uses full fine-tuning (3 epochs), Gemma uses LoRA (1 epoch); Qwen fine-tuned but Gemma only zero-shot evaluated
VisualTableQA benchmark underdeveloped: only 306 examples, no inter-annotator agreement, modest improvements (47.8% vs 41.1%), no performance breakdown by question type
Limited error analysis and ablations: only ablates interpretation tasks; doesn't explain which visual features drive improvements or why interpretation tasks help downstream performance
Computational cost prohibitive: TABLET-L training requires 125 GPU hours on 32 A100s, limiting reproducibility and accessibility

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important gap: clearly demonstrates that existing VTU datasets use synthetic table renderings that lack complexity and visual diversity of real-world tables

Large-scale, well-curated resource: 4 million examples across 21 tasks grounded in 2 million unique tables with 88% preserving original visualizations—substantial improvement over MMTab's synthetic approach
Strong empirical validation of core claim: Table 2 shows training on original visualizations reduces robustness degradation from 28.9 to 6.63 percentage points when generalizing to real tables
Comprehensive experimental validation: systematic evaluation across 15 benchmarks (8 held-in, 7 held-out) with multiple models and training regimes, demonstrating consistent transfer to unseen tasks

Thoughtful dataset design: maintains full traceability to source datasets, provides both image and HTML representations, unified instruction format, metadata with archival links enabling reproducibility and future extensions
Introduces VisualTableQA benchmark: 306 manually-curated examples requiring genuine joint visual-semantic reasoning, with 13% relative improvement over zero-shot
Excellent reproducibility: detailed methodology for retrieving original Wikipedia tables, complete hyperparameter specifications, code and data promised for release
Strong robustness analysis: visual complexity metric (Appendix 10) demonstrates models remain robust as table complexity increases, with clear visualization across all benchmarks
Practical ablations: analyzes dataset composition (Table Interpretation tasks, balanced vs. full distributions), TABLET-M vs TABLET-L tradeoffs
Well-executed scientific approach: appropriate statistical testing mentioned, clear experimental design with well-motivated choices
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily a data aggregation and curation effort rather than introducing new algorithms, architectures, or training techniques—contribution is in data collection rather than methods

Data contamination with pre-training not fully addressed: most seed datasets from Wikipedia (61.5%), and Qwen2.5-VL likely encountered Wikipedia during pre-training, raising questions about whether improvements stem from TABLET's quality or distributional overlap
Incomplete experimental analysis: authors acknowledge skipping full task-level ablations due to computational constraints; individual task contribution analysis would clarify improvement drivers
Limited task innovation: only 1 genuinely new task (VisualTableQA with 306 examples); remaining 20 tasks reformatted from existing datasets rather than novel task design

VisualTableQA benchmark limitations: very small (306 examples), no inter-annotator agreement metrics, single-annotator curation introduces bias, question categories partially overlap with existing reasoning types

Modest improvements on held-in tasks: improvements inconsistent across benchmarks (e.g., WikiTQ degrades from TABLET-M to TABLET-L in Table 3), suggesting benefits primarily manifest in robustness rather than absolute performance
Evaluation scope limitations: restricted to open-weight models (Qwen2.5-VL, Gemma-3); no comparison with proprietary models (GPT-4V, Claude) that dominate in practice
Practical utility questions: TABLET-M performs comparably to TABLET-L on many tasks, yet full dataset requires significant computational resources; unclear if largest variant is necessary
Limited characterization of when/why original visualizations matter: Table 2 isolates robustness benefits well, but paper lacks analysis of task properties that benefit most from visual features

Technical design choices insufficiently justified: similarity threshold of 0.7 for Wikipedia matching lacks sensitivity analysis; visual complexity metric's 9 weighted components lack ablation studies
